analysis.one_liner: Bans selling or sharing identifiable health data collected by smartwatches and fitness trackers for commercial gain.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan SMARTWATCH Data Act, which would have barred selling wearable health data to data brokers, never got a committee vote after being referred to the Senate HELP Committee on March 1, 2021 [S5].
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for companies that collect health data from consumer devices like smartwatches and fitness trackers to sell or share that identifiable data with data brokers or other companies for commercial purposes [S2][S3]. It allowed exceptions, including when a consumer gives informed consent, and it made health data from wearables that reaches doctors or insurers subject to existing federal medical-privacy rules [S2][S3]. HHS would have enforced the restrictions the same way it enforces HIPAA privacy rules [S3]. The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and never advanced [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who wears a smartwatch or fitness tracker. The bill would have stopped their heart rate, sleep, location-derived movement patterns, and other health signals from being sold to data brokers and advertisers without real consent [S3]. Because that data can reveal sensitive conditions, pregnancy, and daily routines, keeping it out of commercial resale protects people from profiling, discrimination risks, and unwanted targeted advertising.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits transferring, selling, or sharing identifiable consumer health information from personal devices to domestic data brokers or other for-profit entities, unless an exception applies such as informed consent [S3].
Blocks transfers of consumer device health data to foreign entities unless strong privacy and security protections are in place [S2][S3].

Makes wearable health data that reaches health care providers, health plans, or their business associates protected health information under existing federal privacy standards, closing a gap where such data currently falls outside HIPAA [S2][S3].
Sets HHS as the enforcer, applying the same penalties and enforcement machinery used for HIPAA privacy violations [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers and analytics firms that currently buy or license this data would lose a supply. Wearable device and app companies would face restrictions on monetizing user health data and new compliance duties. Some free or low-cost services subsidized by data monetization could see that business model curtailed.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers and wearable tech companies

drawbacks.text: The exceptions are broad: data can still be shared with affiliates and 'trusted businesses,' in mergers and bankruptcy sales, and with government and law enforcement, so a company with expansive corporate ties could move data through those channels [S3].
The bill only covers data created by consumer devices, leaving the much larger universe of health data from other sources, such as apps and websites not tied to a device, untouched [S3].
Compliance costs for device makers and health-related app developers could be passed on to consumers or reduce free product features.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection addresses a real gap: health data from wearables is currently outside HIPAA and can be sold with little restriction. The costs fall mainly on companies that profit from that data, though the broad exceptions and the narrow device-only scope mean the bill would have been a strong first step rather than comprehensive privacy protection.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced and never received a markup or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Cassidy, the top Republican on the Senate health committee, introduced the bill on March 1, 2021, joined by Sen. Jacky Rosen, a Democrat [S1][S3][S4].
It was read twice and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on March 1, 2021, which was its final action [S5].
No further action, hearing, markup, or vote is recorded for the remainder of the 117th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers, advertisers, and consumer tech companies keep an unrestricted market for wearable health data; consumers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers and wearable tech firms

for.name: Sen. Bill Cassidy
for.role: Senate sponsor; Ranking Member, Senate HELP Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban commercial sale of wearable health data.

against.name: HELP Committee leadership
against.role: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee majority
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or sent it to the floor during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican sponsor (the ranking member of the committee it was referred to) and a Democratic cosponsor introduced it, and no recorded opposition appears in the record; it simply never moved [S1][S4][S5].

industries.note: These companies buy and resell consumer health data from wearables for targeting and profiling; the bill would have cut off that supply unless consumers consented. Their gain comes from monetizing data that reveals people's sensitive health details.

industries.industry: Wearable device and consumer health app companies
industries.note: Restrictions on selling user health data would limit one revenue stream and add compliance duties, while building trust in wearables could support device sales. Companies whose main business is selling hardware gain relatively little; those monetizing data lose more.

industries.industry: Health insurers and health care providers
industries.note: Wearable data they receive would become protected health information subject to HIPAA, adding compliance obligations but also closing a loophole in medical privacy for their patients and members.
